::: {.cite-bar .domain-intelligence}
[Partly expired]{.status .status-partly-expired} [Pub. L. 95-511]{.cite} [92 Stat. 1783]{.cite} [50 U.S.C. 1801 et seq.]{.cite}
:::

Created a judicial process for foreign intelligence surveillance inside the United States. The government must persuade a special court that the target is a foreign power or an agent of one before it may wiretap or search.

## Key provisions

- Title I: electronic surveillance orders from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court on probable cause that the target is a foreign power or its agent.
- Title III (1994): physical searches. Title IV (1998): pen registers and trap-and-trace devices. Title V (1998): business records.
- Minimization procedures limit retention and sharing of information about U.S. persons.
- Declared to be the exclusive means for covered foreign intelligence surveillance.

## Why it matters

Enacted after the Church Committee documented decades of warrantless surveillance of Americans. It is the base statute that the [USA PATRIOT Act](patriot-2001.qmd), [the FISA Amendments Act](fisa-amendments-2008.qmd), the [USA FREEDOM Act](usa-freedom-2015.qmd), and [RISAA](risaa-2024.qmd) all amend.

## Current status

The core titles on electronic surveillance, physical search, and pen registers are in force. Title VII, including Section 702, lapsed in June 2026 (see the FISA Amendments Act page). The business records, roving wiretap, and lone wolf provisions lapsed in March 2020.
